course: Basic First Aid for Business and Community

lessons.title: Recognizing Cardiac Arrest and Agonal Breathing
lessons.body: Cardiac arrest happens when the heart suddenly stops pumping blood. In Africa, it often occurs outside hospitals, in homes, markets, and workplaces. Every minute without CPR reduces survival by about 10%. You must act fast. The first step is to check for responsiveness. Tap the person firmly on the shoulder and shout, 'Are you okay?' If they do not respond, they may be in cardiac arrest. Next, check for normal breathing. Look at the chest for 5 to 10 seconds. A person in cardiac arrest may have no breathing or only gasping. Gasping, also called agonal breathing, looks like occasional snoring, gurgling, or slow, irregular gasps. It is not normal breathing. Many people mistake gasping for normal breathing and delay CPR. Do not be fooled. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, assume cardiac arrest. In Africa, common causes include heart attacks, electrocution, drowning, and severe allergic reactions. Business owners and community members should be trained to recognize these signs. Remember: unresponsive + no normal breathing = start CPR. Call for help immediately. If you are alone, use your mobile phone to call emergency services on speaker while you begin CPR. In many African countries, emergency numbers vary: 112 in Kenya, 10111 in South Africa, 199 in Nigeria. Know your local number. Do not waste time checking for a pulse; it is unreliable even for trained professionals. The key is to recognize the absence of normal breathing and act. Time is heart muscle. Every second counts.

lessons.title: Hands-Only CPR Technique for Adults
lessons.body: Hands-only CPR is CPR without rescue breaths. It is recommended for untrained bystanders or those unwilling to give breaths. It is simple, effective, and easy to remember. For adults, hands-only CPR can double or triple survival chances. Here is how to do it. First, ensure the scene is safe. Then, tap the person and shout. If no response and no normal breathing, call for help. If someone else is around, ask them to call emergency services and find an AED. If you are alone, call on speakerphone and start CPR. Position the person on their back on a firm, flat surface. Kneel beside their chest. Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, between the nipples. Place your other hand on top and interlock your fingers. Keep your arms straight, shoulders directly above your hands. Push hard and fast. Compress at least 5 cm (2 inches) deep. Push at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. That is about 2 compressions per second. Allow the chest to come back up fully after each compression. Do not stop until help arrives, an AED is ready, or you are too exhausted to continue. In Africa, many people fear causing harm, but doing nothing is worse. Hands-only CPR is safe and does not require mouth-to-mouth. It is perfect for busy markets, offices, and community gatherings. Practice on a pillow or a CPR manikin if available. The rhythm of the song 'Stayin' Alive' by the Bee Gees is about 100 beats per minuteâuse it to keep pace. Remember: push hard, push fast, and do not stop.

lessons.title: Chest Compressions: Depth, Rate, and Recoil
lessons.body: Chest compressions are the heart of CPR. They manually pump blood to the brain and vital organs. To be effective, you must get three things right: depth, rate, and recoil. Depth: For an average adult, push down at least 5 cm (2 inches) but not more than 6 cm (2.4 inches). If you are a small person, use your body weight to help. Too shallow and blood flow is poor; too deep and you may break ribs. Rib fractures are a risk, but they are better than death. Rate: Aim for 100 to 120 compressions per minute. That is faster than one per second. Count out loud: 'One and two and three and...' or use a metronome app. Many smartphones have free metronome apps. The song 'Stayin' Alive' has the correct beat. Recoil: After each compression, let the chest come all the way back up. Do not lean on the chest. This allows the heart to refill with blood. If you do not allow full recoil, blood flow decreases. In Africa, where ambulances may be far away, high-quality compressions are even more critical. You may need to continue for 10, 20, or 30 minutes. Switch with another rescuer every 2 minutes to avoid fatigue. Fatigue leads to shallow compressions. If you are alone, keep going as long as you can. Remember: 5 cm deep, 100-120 per minute, full recoil. Practice on a firm surface. Do not be afraid to push hard. The life you save could be a family member, a colleague, or a customer.

lessons.title: Rescue Breaths: When and How to Provide
lessons.body: Rescue breaths, also called mouth-to-mouth, provide oxygen to a person who is not breathing. In adult CPR, the current recommendation is to start with 30 chest compressions before giving 2 rescue breaths. This is called the 30:2 ratio. However, if you are untrained or uncomfortable, hands-only CPR is still effective. Rescue breaths are especially important for drowning, electrocution, and drug overdose, where lack of oxygen is the main problem. Here is how to give them. First, open the airway. Place one hand on the forehead and two fingers under the chin. Tilt the head back gently. This lifts the tongue away from the back of the throat. Pinch the nose shut with your thumb and index finger. Take a normal breath, not a deep one. Seal your mouth over the person's mouth. Blow steadily for about 1 second. Watch for the chest to rise. If it rises, give a second breath. If it does not rise, re-tilt the head and try again. Do not blow too hard or too fast; it can cause stomach inflation. After 2 breaths, immediately resume compressions. Continue cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths. In Africa, concerns about diseases like HIV and TB may make you hesitant. Use a CPR face shield or pocket mask if available. If not, you can still do hands-only CPR. The risk of transmission is very low. If you are unwilling or unable to give breaths, do not stop compressions. Something is better than nothing. Remember: 30 compressions, 2 breaths, repeat.

lessons.title: Using an AED: Pad Placement and Safety
lessons.body: An AED, or Automated External Defibrillator, is a portable device that checks the heart rhythm and can send an electric shock to restart the heart. It is safe and easy to use, even for untrained people. AEDs are increasingly available in African airports, malls, and large offices. If you see one, use it. First, turn on the AED. It will give you voice prompts. Expose the person's chest. Dry it if wet. Remove any medication patches. If the person has a lot of chest hair, shave it quickly with a razor from the AED kit. Place one pad on the upper right side of the chest, just below the collarbone. Place the other pad on the lower left side, below the nipple, on the side of the chest. The pads have pictures to guide you. Plug the connector into the AED if not already connected. The AED will analyze the heart rhythm. Do not touch the person during analysis. If a shock is advised, the AED will charge. Shout 'Clear!' and make sure no one is touching the person. Press the shock button. Immediately resume chest compressions after the shock. If no shock is advised, continue CPR. The AED will re-analyze every 2 minutes. Keep the pads on. In Africa, AEDs may be rare, but if one is available, it greatly improves survival. Do not be afraid to use it. It will not shock a normal heart. Remember: turn on, attach pads, clear, shock if advised, resume CPR.

lessons.title: Team CPR and Switching Roles
lessons.body: Cardiac arrest is a team effort. When more than one rescuer is available, you can provide better CPR with less fatigue. The key is to switch roles every 2 minutes, or sooner if tired. High-quality compressions require energy. After 2 minutes, even a strong person starts to push less deeply. So, plan your team. One person does compressions. Another gives rescue breaths. A third calls emergency services and finds an AED. A fourth can manage the crowd and keep time. If you have only two rescuers, one does compressions while the other gives breaths. Switch every 2 minutes. The switch should be quickâless than 5 seconds. To switch smoothly, the rescuer doing compressions says, 'I'm getting tired, switch on my next count.' Then, at the end of a cycle, the new rescuer kneels on the opposite side, places hands on the chest, and continues. The old rescuer moves to the breathing position. If you are alone, you cannot switch, but you can call for help. In African communities, teamwork is natural. Use it. Appoint a timekeeper with a phone timer. Rotate roles. Keep encouraging each other. After the ambulance arrives, give a clear handover: what happened, when CPR started, how many shocks, and any changes. Remember: 2-minute switches, clear communication, and support. Team CPR saves more lives than solo CPR. Practice with your colleagues, family, or community group. You never know when you will need it.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should do if you see someone collapse?
options: B) Tap and shout to check responsiveness
quiz.explanation: Checking responsiveness helps you determine if the person needs CPR.

quiz.q: What does agonal breathing look like?
options: C) Occasional gasps or snoring sounds
quiz.explanation: Agonal breathing is irregular gasping and is a sign of cardiac arrest.

quiz.q: If an adult is unresponsive and not breathing normally, what should you assume?
options: B) They are having a seizure
C) They are in cardiac arrest
quiz.explanation: Unresponsiveness with abnormal breathing indicates cardiac arrest.

quiz.q: What is the recommended compression depth for adult CPR?
quiz.explanation: Compressions should be at least 5 cm deep for effective blood flow.

quiz.q: What is the correct compression rate for adult CPR?
quiz.explanation: 100-120 compressions per minute is the recommended rate.

quiz.q: What does 'recoil' mean in chest compressions?
options: B) Letting the chest come back up fully
quiz.explanation: Full recoil allows the heart to refill with blood.

quiz.q: What is the compression-to-breath ratio for adult CPR with rescue breaths?
quiz.explanation: The standard ratio is 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

quiz.q: When should you use hands-only CPR?
options: B) If you are untrained or unwilling to give breaths
quiz.explanation: Hands-only CPR is recommended for untrained bystanders.

quiz.q: How long should each rescue breath last?
quiz.explanation: Each breath should be given over about 1 second to avoid stomach inflation.

quiz.q: What should you do if the chest does not rise during rescue breaths?
options: B) Re-tilt the head and try again
quiz.explanation: Re-tilting the head opens the airway so the breath can go in.

quiz.q: What does AED stand for?
quiz.explanation: AED stands for Automated External Defibrillator.

quiz.q: Where should you place the AED pads on an adult?
options: A) Both on the left side
B) One on upper right chest, one on lower left side
C) One on the back, one on the front
D) Both on the right side
quiz.explanation: This placement allows the shock to pass through the heart.

quiz.q: What should you do before pressing the shock button on an AED?
options: B) Shout 'Clear!' and ensure no one is touching the person
quiz.explanation: Shouting 'Clear!' prevents anyone from being shocked.

quiz.q: After an AED shock, what should you do immediately?
quiz.explanation: Immediately resume compressions to keep blood flowing.

quiz.q: How often should you switch roles during team CPR?
quiz.explanation: Switching every 2 minutes prevents fatigue and maintains compression quality.

quiz.q: What is the recommended emergency number in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: 112 is the emergency number in Kenya and many other countries.

quiz.q: Why is it important to allow full chest recoil?
options: B) To let the heart refill with blood
quiz.explanation: Full recoil allows blood to return to the heart.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are alone and find an unresponsive adult?
options: B) Call emergency services on speaker and start CPR
C) Check for a pulse for 1 minute
D) Wait for someone to come
quiz.explanation: Calling on speaker allows you to start CPR immediately.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common cause of cardiac arrest in Africa?
quiz.explanation: All these can cause cardiac arrest.

quiz.q: What is the song often used to keep the correct compression rate?
quiz.explanation: 'Stayin' Alive' has about 100 beats per minute.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are unwilling to give rescue breaths?
quiz.explanation: Hands-only CPR is still effective and recommended.

quiz.q: What is the maximum compression depth for an adult?
quiz.explanation: Compressions should not exceed 6 cm to avoid injury.

quiz.q: What should you do if the AED says 'no shock advised'?
quiz.explanation: Continue CPR until help arrives or the person starts breathing.

quiz.q: How many rescuers are ideal for team CPR?
quiz.explanation: 3 or more allows for role rotation and less fatigue.

quiz.q: What should you do before placing AED pads on a hairy chest?
options: D) Place pads on the back
quiz.explanation: Shaving ensures good pad contact.

quiz.q: What is the first step when using an AED?
quiz.explanation: Turning on the AED starts the voice prompts.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid leaning on the chest between compressions?
quiz.explanation: Leaning prevents the chest from coming back up, reducing blood flow.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are alone and have an AED?
options: A) Use it immediately without CPR
B) Start CPR, then use AED as soon as possible
D) Only use AED after 10 minutes
quiz.explanation: CPR first, then AED as soon as it is available.

quiz.q: What is the role of the timekeeper in team CPR?
options: C) To keep track of 2-minute cycles
quiz.explanation: The timekeeper ensures rescuers switch every 2 minutes.

quiz.q: What should you do if the person starts breathing normally during CPR?
quiz.explanation: If normal breathing returns, stop CPR and monitor until help arrives.
